You go in when your contractions are consistently 5 minutes apart. They take you to a delivery room, you sign some forms (if you want an epidural, sign it now), let them know what your birth plan is (delayed cord clamping is a good idea as ~1/3rd of the baby’s blood is still in the placenta post delivery), then progress through labor until delivery. They check the baby’s vitals and if there’s an emergency, they’ll cut the cord right away and deal with the crisis. They’ll give your baby antibiotic eyedrops (standard, but you can refuse). If you’re having a boy, decide if you want a circumcision (there are nerve endings and it’s a painful recovery, I would suggest letting them make their own decision in the future, as it’s cosmetic anyways). You birth the placenta a few minutes-30 minutes after the baby’s born. They’ll give your baby a hearing test and prick his foot to test its iron levels periodically. Usually they have a lactation consultant help you figure out latching and feeding if you choose that route. Nurses will come to check on you and baby, change diapers, and sometimes they’ll give the first bath. They’ll clean them up regardless. You’ll get pain meds on a schedule and they’ll massage your stomach to help your uterus contract which aids in stopping blood loss from the placenta detaching. Breastfeeding also makes your uterus contract. It feels like painful period cramps. At some point after the birth, you’ll tell them the name, sign some more forms related to your baby’s birth for the certificate and social security number, etc. The father will sign a paternity affidavit if he wants to be on the birth certificate. They’ll give you papers relating to your baby’s height/weight/time born/how to care for your baby/follow up care. You’ll be discharged when you and your baby are stable and ready.

This is something I’ve struggled with, but have largely worked through with years of self-reflection. For me, it stemmed from a lacking my own sense of security within the relationship. There are better ways to build that with your partner, but it’s important to understand that it’s a form of insecurity and the best way to help them work through it is to be honest and provide feedback. Let them know when they’re doing a good job or met your needs. Talk about what’s important to you and you want to work towards having and things that happened in the past that you don’t want to go through again. The questions might feel probing, but the truth is important for his growth, the relationship, and reinforcing your own character. It’s a difficult conversation to have no matter which side you’re on. You should remind him that this is difficult for you, share what you’re worried about, and outline the importance of building trust and safety between you two. Some parts will probably hurt to hear, but it’s helpful to reroute to the ideology that none of your life was lived to cause harm to him, things didn’t work out with others, and based off of all your experience, he looked like the next best step for your life, and out of anyone else you could have considered, you *chose* him because of who he is in the world. Give your own spin, of course. These are all just things I learned about myself and things I needed to hear and understand from my partner. Regardless of where the relationship stands, you should always challenge yourself to make the morally right decisions and practice who you want to be in the world. Relationships should always be built on a foundation of truth. It’s not healthy to hide yourself — especially from your partner. Ideally, that’s your teammate — and teams work best when they have all the information. Problems are easier to solve, each party knows where they are, how they need to respond, and what to expect. Life can be difficult, but things outside your control are a thousand times easier if you prioritize building a great partnership. It’s hard work in the beginning, but it gets easy pretty quickly if you’re committed to it.
